Chapter 11 · Birth of the discipline · 1890–1920

Consciousness, introspection and functionalism

Titchener looked for the elements of consciousness; William James asked what it is for. The debate that shaped the first academic psychology.

With the first laboratories, psychology had a place of its own. What it still had to agree on was what exactly it should study. Around 1900 two answers clashed: describe consciousness by breaking it down into its elements, or ask what it is for and how it helps us adapt.

What were people trying to understand?

What conscious experience is made of, whether all thought is accompanied by images, how habits are formed and what role the mind plays in people's practical lives.

With what methods?

The main tool was introspection, but not in the everyday sense of "looking inwards". Edward Titchener, Wundt's English student who settled at Cornell University, trained his observers over thousands of trials to describe sensations, images and feelings without interpreting them. He called his programme structuralism and catalogued more than 40,000 distinct sensory qualities.

In Germany, Oswald Külpe and his colleagues in Würzburg asked participants to solve tasks and then report what had gone through their minds. Many said they had thought without any concrete image or sensation. That conclusion, imageless thought, clashed with Titchener, and the dispute could not be settled: each laboratory found what its method trained it to see.

Who took part?

In the United States, William James published The Principles of Psychology in 1890, two volumes that took him twelve years to write. He described consciousness as a "stream", continuous and changing, not a mosaic of pieces. He wrote about habit, attention, memory, the self and emotion, and argued with Carl Lange that we feel emotion by perceiving changes in the body, not the other way round.

Functionalism grew out of his work. John Dewey criticised in 1896 the idea of a reflex arc made of separate pieces and proposed seeing it as a coordinated circuit. James Rowland Angell, in Chicago, defined psychology as the study of mental functions in the service of adaptation. G. Stanley Hall founded the American Psychological Association (APA) in 1892 and studied adolescence. Mary Whiton Calkins invented the paired-associates method for studying memory and in 1905 became the first woman president of the APA, although Harvard refused her a doctorate because she was a woman. Margaret Floy Washburn was the first woman to earn a doctorate in psychology in the United States and wrote The Animal Mind (1908).

What did it contribute?

  • A vocabulary for describing experience, and experiments on sensation and attention that are still cited.
  • The functional question, "what is it for?", which opened the way to applied, educational and comparative psychology.
  • Topics that remain central to the discipline: habit, attention, memory, emotion and the self.
  • The first scientific societies and journals of psychology.

What was revised later?

Structuralism all but vanished with Titchener's death in 1927. Trained introspection proved unreliable for settling disagreements, and that weakness was the behaviourists' main argument for abandoning it. Even so, verbal reports returned to cognitive psychology with more careful controls, and the James–Lange theory of emotion has come back, in qualified form, in current research on interoception. Wundt, incidentally, never held the structuralism that Titchener spread in his name.

"Consciousness does not appear to itself chopped up in bits. It is nothing jointed; it flows" (William James, 1890).
